guard: the `input` op authorizes exactly as `attach` does before it writes, `enter:false` suppresses the carriage return, and a sent receipt comes only from the runtime's acknowledged write
why: Two cells carry the whole feature's risk and they fail in opposite directions, so each is
aimed at separately rather than trusting one kill to speak for the suite.
AUTHORIZATION is the one that fails toward harm. `input` writes into somebody's running agent,
so a handler that answered before checking would let any spawn-capable credential type into any
seat on the manager. The refusal cell would still be there, still named, and still green if the
check moved, was reordered after the write, or was deleted in a refactor that kept the shape.
THE CARRIAGE RETURN is the one that fails toward a wrong result rather than a loud one. It is a
one-character ternary; flipping it makes `enter:false` submit the line anyway, which for a
harness command means the command RUNS when the caller asked to stage it. Nothing about that
looks broken from the reply, which reports a byte count the mutant would also compute.
SPECIFIER BOUNDARY, checked rather than assumed. The suite imports `../src/manager.js`, which
tsx resolves to the SOURCE file both mutations edit, so the bytes mutated are the bytes
executed and no build step is needed. Cell 8 spawns the real `bin/cotal.ts`, whose CLIENT half
(flag parsing, the mint, the subject) does ride `dist` and is therefore NOT what either
mutation edits; the manager that cell reaches is the same in-process source manager as every
other cell, so a manager-side mutation is visible there too. Measured: both kills dropped more
progress marks than the one named cell accounts for.
The suite therefore straddles TWO specifiers at once, and the placement guard is the cell that
depends on the other one. Cell 9 asks whether a spawn-only credential's minted grant carries an
`input` row, and that mint comes from `@cotal-ai/core`, which resolves to its DIST. Review hit
exactly this locally: a source tree already narrowed, a dist still holding the old
`["despawn","attach","input"]`, and cell 9 red in a shape that reads like a product defect (the
owner-mode publish is ALLOWED and the handler answers permission-denied, while the any-mode
publish is still broker-dropped). CI cannot reproduce it: the smoke job builds before sharding
and every shard is a fresh checkout. Named here so a future local red on cell 9 is diagnosed as a
stale dist in one step instead of being chased into the manager.
THE READINESS GATE IS NOT MUTATION-PROVABLE, and it is named here rather than left to look
graded. `spawnLive` blocks on a marker the child writes only after raw mode and its stdin reader
are in place, because the manager lists a seat in `ps` from the moment it LAUNCHES the process:
review measured a one-in-six false red where the first keystroke landed on a still-cooked tty.
A mutation that deletes the gate does not redden deterministically, since what it removes is a
race, and a mutation that deletes the marker does not redden a named CELL either, it makes the
suite unable to start. What IS structural: the marker's absence stops the suite at `spawnLive`
with a FIXTURE FAILURE rather than letting a cell pass, and cell 1 asserts the marker exists, so
a dead mechanism cannot be mistaken for a satisfied one.
THE ACKNOWLEDGED RECEIPT is the issue #1333 honesty boundary. The dropped-write cell replaces
the live handle write with a resolved no-op carrying no accepted-byte count. The real CLI must
exit non-zero, name the seat and the acknowledgement failure, print no `sent` receipt, and the
child must receive nothing. Its mutation restores the old intended-buffer arithmetic, which
turns that same cell back into the exact false success reported by triage.
NOT GRADED HERE, and named rather than implied: the refusal for a runtime with no `write` on
its handle. That branch is reached by ABSENCE of an optional method, which no mutation of this
source can produce and no fixture in this suite can spawn, so it is covered by the type and by
the handler's own `if (!write)` rather than by a kill.

mutations.name: the return is fused back onto the text, so a seat submits one call behind (issue #1649)
mutations.expectRed: THE RETURN WAS WRITTEN ALONE, AFTER the paste close: the harness is handed a submit key, not a pasted newline
mutations.cell: THE RETURN WAS WRITTEN ALONE, AFTER the paste close: the harness is handed a submit key, not a pasted newline
mutations.note: The shipped defect, restored exactly: one write carrying the text and its return. The BYTES are identical either way, so the sink cells cannot see it and stay green - that is why #1649 shipped and why this mutation is worth a row. A TUI harness reads keystrokes, so a fused return is the text's last character rather than the submit key: the line waits in the composer and the next call's return submits the previous call's text, while the op reports the full byte count and the seat still starts a turn. Only the write shape separates them, which is why cell 10 records what the handler hands the pty through a pass-through rather than reading the child's sink. This mutation also reds the 4096-byte slice assertion, because the fused form re-introduces the oversized single write the kernel re-splits. Re-anchored onto a CODE-ONLY window: the previous target spanned the `enter:false` comment, so a prose tidy could have disarmed it. The window now starts at the separate-return write and rebuilds `parts` into the single fused write, which is byte-for-byte the shipped defect the previous `replace` produced (text and its return in one write, no bracketed paste framing, no slicing).

mutations.name: the paste framing is dropped, keeping the lone return, so a multi-write text is still one call behind (issue #1649)
mutations.expectRed: the child received the text wrapped in paste markers with the return after the close marker
mutations.cell: the child received the text wrapped in paste markers with the return after the close marker
mutations.note: The SECOND half of #1649, and the one that survived the first fix. Separating the return is necessary but not sufficient: a TUI classifies a fast burst as a paste and consumes the newline trailing it, so any text long enough to need more than one write still sat in the composer until the NEXT call's return. Measured on a real jcode seat through a real pty with this exact mutant shape: 120 and 700 bytes submitted on their own call, while 2500 and 3100 bytes did not, each appearing only on the following call. The end-to-end proof is `implementations/manager/smoke/acceptance-1649-e2e.mjs`, which went from `submitted match [true,true,false]` to `[true,true,true]` when the markers were added.
